newsitem.title: INDIA: Analysts keep hopes as Indian government teeters.
newsitem.headline: Analysts keep hopes as Indian government teeters.

text.p: While India's minority coalition teetered ahead of a confidence vote on Friday, foreign investor analysts clung to hopes that the end-game in political brinkmanship was still to be played.
"It looks like a mid-term election is most likely," Alok Sethi, director of NatWest Markets in Bombay, told Reuters on Thursday.

"But my gut feeling is that these guys still have something up their sleeve. It is brinkmanship, and they could come up with something by 11 a.m. tomorrow (0530 GMT). If not we're in for mid-term polls," he said.
India looks as if it will be handicapped by political risk and another period without a government capable of taking tough decisions, analysts said.

Over the short term foreign institutional investors in India have taken a battering, but Finance Minister P. Chidambaram's growth and business-friendly budget announced on February 28 raised hopes of money-making times ahead.
Now the budget is hostage to the fate of the government, and investment commitments are either withheld or small.

The high drama in New Delhi kept Indian markets twitching on Thursday with each fresh story, or rumour coming out of a meeting between United Front (UF) government negotiators and counterparts from its erstwhile ally in the Congress party.
The Bombay Stock Exchange's top-30 share index ended 52.51 points, or 1.44 percent, lower at 3,598.37 after dipping to 3,554.77.
"We are still adopting a wait and watch attitude," said the director of another foreign investment house in Bombay, adding, "But today's events shook confidence a bit."
UF leaders told Congress that they will not dump Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, the price demanded by their former allies for renewing support of the government.
Congress withdrew its backing for the 15-member coalition on March 30, accusing the government of fostering communalism and allowing the economy to drift.

Since then, there has been little talk of these issues and the political dogfight has boiled down to power and personalities, and left pundits still puzzling over why Congress leader Sitaram Kesri precipitated the crisis, analysts said.
"They haven't really left room for a face-saving compromise. No-one wants to commit suicide by abject surrender," Prashant Purker, head of institutional sales at Peregrine Capital India Pvt Ltd said.
Congress leaders talked about their willingness to negotiate a power sharing deal with the UF once the government, and Deve Gowda had been defeated.

Purker warned against assuming the government will lose Friday's vote, pointing out that the opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the largest single party in the Lok Sabha (Lower House) has still to definitively say how it will vote.
"The BJP has still not announced whether it will oppose, support or abstain," he said.
If the BJP does not vote against the government it can always wait to choose its own time to sink the coalition later, he said.
"In our opinion an election might not be a bad idea to get the uncertainty out of the way, provided the winners get a clear mandate this time, even if it is the BJP," NatWest's Sethi said.
Analysts also raised the possibility that Congress could end up being split over the attack on the government, and some members could come over to the UF camp, reinforcing the government.
Whatever happens on Friday India will be unable to recapture the fragile political balance it had before March 30.
"The uncertainty is bound to continue beyond Friday, even if a compromise is reached tomorrow," Purker said.
Sethi said some investment houses were already trimming earnings growth forecasts based on the foggy political scene.
The long term investor is likely to become very selective and buy in defensive sectors, he said.
